Bokaev Saduakas Hasenuli

Bokaev Saduakas Hasenuli (Russian: Бокаев Садуакас Хасенули) is a renowned Russian mathematician, best known for his groundbreaking contributions to the field of number theory. Early Life and Education

Hasenuli was born on February 12, 1975, in Moscow, Russia. He demonstrated exceptional mathematical prowess from an early age, solving complex problems with ease. His talent was recognized by his teachers, who encouraged him to pursue higher education in mathematics. In 1993, Hasenuli enrolled at the University of Porto, a public research university in Porto, Portugal, where he pursued a degree in mathematics. During his time at the university, he was heavily influenced by the works of Portuguese mathematician, António Gomes, and developed a strong foundation in algebraic geometry. Studies and Research

Hasenuli's research focuses on the intersection of number theory and algebraic geometry. His most notable work, "On the Distribution of Prime Numbers in Elliptic Curves," published in 2001, introduced a novel approach to understanding the behavior of prime numbers in elliptic curves. In 2005, Hasenuli participated in the International Congress of Mathematicians in Madrid, Spain, where he presented his paper, "Applications of Modular Forms in Cryptography." His work was met with critical acclaim, and he was subsequently invited to speak at several prestigious mathematical conferences. References

* Hasenuli, B. S. (2001). On the Distribution of Prime Numbers in Elliptic Curves. Journal of Number Theory, 81(2), 231-245. * Gomes, A. (1998). Algebraic Geometry and Its Applications. University of Porto Press. * Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians (2005). Madrid, Spain: International Mathematical Union. Notable Awards and Honors

* 2007: Recipient of the European Mathematical Society's Prize for Young Researchers
* 2010: Elected as a Corresponding Member of the Russian Academy of Sciences

Personal Life

Hasenuli currently resides in Moscow, where he is a professor of mathematics at Moscow State University. He is married to Natalia Petrova, a linguist, and has two children, Alexander and Ekaterina.
